note: How a refusal is worded, asserted by both surfaces against this one file.
`parity/cases.json` pins rules across two LANGUAGES. This pins one rule
across two SURFACES: `apps/web/src/lib/describe.ts` and
`apps/mobile/src/describe.ts` are the same function word for word, because
the two answer to the same API and somebody who meets a limit on their
phone and then on their laptop should not be told two different things
about it. The phone's file claimed that parity in a comment while the web
had a dozen hand-rolled versions, several of which threw the server's own
sentence away and blamed the network. This is what makes the claim true.
Hand-written, unlike `cases.json`: there is no generator, because there is
no second implementation to generate it from — only two copies of one.
`errors` is the API's validation bag; `message` is its top-level sentence.
A case with neither stands for a request that never got an answer.
`load` is the second function in that file: the sentence a screen shows
when it could not load what it is about. `Could not load your journal.` is
a statement about an absence and saying it is right; the reason after it
has to be the server's. Five screens bound the error and threw it away,
then blamed the connection for a request that had arrived — and CLAUDE.md
excused them as having no error to describe, which was false for those
five. The connection case drops `describe()`'s opening clause, since this
has already said what failed.

cases.why: What a 500 actually looks like. Measured with `app.debug` off, which is what a deployment runs: Laravel answers `Server Error` for anything that is not an HttpException. This case used to carry an empty message — a shape a deployment never sends — and so agreed with the wrong answer.
